passage: Rehana, you say you spend an hour every evening deciding when to start? Let me tell you about my board year. I am Nikita, and I used to negotiate with myself daily: after a snack, after a call, after the news. The evening would slip away. Then one night I wrote a single sentence on a card: "When it is six o'clock and my chai is finished, I open Physics at my desk." No decision, only a cue. The first evening felt silly. By the third, my hand reached for the book as soon as the cup was empty, and Amma, who brought the chai, found it already open when she came to collect the cup. The debate ended because there was nothing left to debate.

qa.q: What sentence did Nikita write on the card?
qa.a: Nikita wrote "When it is six o'clock and my chai is finished, I open Physics at my desk."

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling about the daily debate over starting?
qa.a: Frustrated, since the evening kept slipping away while Nikita bargained.

qa.q: What other cue could Nikita have used?
qa.a: Right after washing the dinner plates, because any fixed daily event can act as a starter.

qa.q: How might Amma have seen the change in the evenings?
qa.a: Probably with relief and curiosity, since the book was already open when Amma came to collect the cup.

grounding: A student decides in advance that at six with the chai finished the Physics book opens, so the daily debate disappears.

passage: Every evening Usha lost an hour to the same argument with herself: start now, or after one more video, or after Ojas stops practising the harmonium in the next room. The Physics paper was five weeks away and the argument was winning. On Sunday she sat on the balcony and thought it through. Deciding every day is the problem. So I decide once. If it's six and my chai cup is empty, Physics comes out on the desk. Harmonium or no harmonium. She wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it on the cup. On Monday at six, Ojas was halfway through a very loud scale. Usha drained her chai, looked at the note and walked to the desk. Earplugs in. Book open, chapter four. No debate.

qa.q: What was Ojas doing at six on Monday?
qa.a: He was halfway through a very loud scale on the harmonium.

qa.q: Why did Usha decide to decide only once?
qa.a: She was frustrated at losing an hour every evening to the start-now-or-later argument, and wanted a rule that ended it.

qa.q: What could Usha do if the six o'clock chai sometimes runs late?
qa.a: Keep the cue but add a backup, such as opening the book at quarter past six even without chai, so the plan doesn't hang on one detail.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Usha's new routine?
qa.a: Ojas may barely notice, or feel a little guilty about the noise, but the plan works whether or not the practice goes on.

grounding: Shows a student deciding in advance that an empty chai cup at six means the Physics book opens, ending the daily debate about starting.

passage: For two weeks, Ramesh's evenings in the Hyderabad flat went the same way. Home at half past five, chai, phone, then "I'll start at seven." Seven became eight. Eight became dinner. On Friday he caught himself arguing with the clock again and stopped. The deciding is what eats the time, he thought. What if I don't decide? What if the chai decides? He tore a page from his rough book and wrote: When it's 6 and the chai is finished, Physics opens at the desk. He stuck it on the fridge, where Pallavi Akka read it aloud in a newsreader voice. Saturday, 6:02, cup empty. He felt the old five-more-minutes tug, looked at the fridge and went. By 6:05 he was drawing ray diagrams.

qa.q: What was Ramesh doing by 6:05 on Saturday?
What did Ramesh feel at 6:02 on Saturday?
qa.a: He felt the old reluctant tug of wanting five more minutes, but the note on the fridge helped him past it.

qa.q: Why might a fixed cue work better for Ramesh than "I'll start at seven"?
qa.a: The cue removes the daily decision: a vague start time invites endless delay, while an empty cup at six is a clear signal to move.

qa.q: How might Pallavi Akka see the note on the fridge?
qa.a: Pallavi Akka finds it funny enough to read in a newsreader voice, but may be impressed when it actually gets him to the desk 🙂.

grounding: Shows a student tying the start of Physics study to a fixed cue, six o'clock and finished chai, to stop the daily debate.
